blogs.title: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026: End User TAB recommendations and tips
blogs.content: Posted on October 29, 2026 by Ricardo Rocha, End User TAB KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City will bring the cloud native community together with projects, vendors and end users in what is one of the largest open source events. In this post, we highlight content specifically targeted at end users and session recommendations from members of the CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board (TAB) , along with practical tips for making the most of the event. Birds of Feather (BoF) Newly introduced at Kubecon EU in Amsterdam back in March, we will again have a series of BoF sessions in Salt Lake City. Last time we had packed rooms discussing and brainstorming around AI infrastructure and platforms, AI observability and optimized infrastructure for training, inference and GPU efficiency. This time around we’ll open the floor to our newly formed end user groups , the TAB recently approved end user groups covering Platform Engineering, Public Sector, Telecom and Research. And in another session we will give ourselves a challenge: get end users in one room and try to build live a reference architecture for Agentic AI deployments. It’s not clear how far we will get given how fast things are moving and how different use cases can be… but it should be a good learning session and it will definitely be fun! Town Hall In Amsterdam we chose to move the End User TAB Town Hall to the project pavilion and that was well received. So we’re keeping it this way and you can come and ask us questions right next to where the projects are located. Poster sessions Did you know Kubecon has a poster session ? It’s an ideal setting to have more in-depth discussions with the authors and there are several end user focused presentations this time around. And as always, see below for recommendations on interesting content for end users from the members of the TAB. Joseph Sandoval Surviving the Churn: Read Replicas and Controllers for Busy Kubernetes Clusters (Nov 10, 12:20 PM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Your apiserver is one ordered log with everyone yelling at it, and when watchers fall behind, they get 410 Gone and relist, which makes it worse. Anthropic’s war story: one innocent LIST sent a cluster of tens of thousands of nodes into a doom spiral, twice in two weeks. Some of us have the scars. N Clusters, One kubectl: Multi-Cluster That Just Works (Nov 10, 3:40 PM, Hyatt Regency, Salt Lake Ballroom C). OCM-style multi-cluster fixes the fleet problem and creates a developer problem: the hub template is the source of truth, so the kubectl scale you just ran quietly gets reverted. Salesforce and NVIDIA built a proxy that makes the fleet feel like one cluster again, kubectl edit included. Every platform fix sends a bill to somebody else, and this talk shows what it took to pay that one down. Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler (Nov 11, 11:00 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom H). Pending workloads timed out webhooks and took down a control plane, which probably looked fine in the design review. Isomorphic Labs and Google walk through how they stabilized it with decoupled queues and Kueue tuning. I’m looking forward to reviewing the receipts. Hardening Kubernetes for GovCloud: A 3-Year Journey to FedRAMP Moderate Authorization (Nov 11, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Three years to an ATO sounds about right to anyone who has argued with an auditor over a deploy pipeline. Kudos to the Verkada team for building their own deployment system to meet the isolation rules, then taking on FedRAMP’s patching mandates. If you work in a regulated environment or are working on it, be front and center for the lessons learned. Juliano Martinez Zero Downtime CNI Migration at Scale: Canal to Cilium Across Hundreds of Production Clusters (Nov 10, 4:40 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, 151). Migrating a CNI plugin in production is one of the most high-risk operations in Kubernetes infra. At Walmart running hundreds of clusters across cloud and on-premises environments, the team faced route-drop failures in Flannel beyond 300 nodes, iptables rule explosion as services grew and etcd v2 incompatibility blocking upgrades. No published playbook existed for zero-downtime CNI replacement at that scale. Saturated by Design – Maximizing Cluster Allocation in On-Premises Kubernetes (Nov 10, 11:30 AM). On-premises compute is inelastic, and the costs are mostly up-front. Yet workload demands and hardware health can change at any time. How do you make the most of your on-premises investments without risking capacity overruns and potential outages? Running Secure Agents at Scale (Nov 11, 5:00 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom GI). Building secure and scalable agents at scale is hard. From multi-tenancy and noisy-neighbor risk to tool access and data boundaries, teams need more than a prompt and a container image; they need a deliberate execution model. From Packets to Paychecks: eBPF-Based Network Cost Attribution at Scale (Nov 12, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom BDF). Cloud provider bills show egress costs as a single line item-they don’t say which tenant caused them. At Adobe, we answer that across 400K pods in 31K namespaces spanning 85+ multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters using Retina eBPF agents to capture pod-level flows at the kernel. Prometheus enriches them with node topology, and a CIDR-based classifier maps each destination IP to a cost category (Local, Internet, Peering, Transit Gateway, VPC Endpoint) with cross-AZ and cross-region modifiers that align to cloud provider billing. Kenta Tada Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent AI agents may look like ordinary Kubernetes workloads, but their long-lived, stateful, and highly privileged behavior makes sandboxing a fundamentally different challenge. This session shares lessons from building agent sandboxing with kagent, covering filesystem and tool access, credentials, networking, identity, and cleanup, along with how NVIDIA’s OpenShell, Kubernetes’ agent-sandbox, and Google’s substrate support shape the design. GPU Observability with eBPF: From Kernel Hooks to Kubernetes Metrics GPUs are becoming a critical resource in Kubernetes, yet understanding what is happening on them remains a black box. This session shows how to build production-grade GPU observability with eBPF, from hooking into GPU interfaces and enriching telemetry with Kubernetes context to packaging programs as OCI images and integrating metrics with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. Chad Beaudin – Boeing Birds of a Feather: Public Sector user Group The Public Sector user group recently went through the new process to be recognized as an official CNCF user group. They have been a healthy user group for a few years and I’m excited to sit in on their BoF session and hear the latest challenges (and solutions!) that leaders in that industry face. Hallway Track It’s cliche for a reason. I get so much value from talking to fellow practitioners at Kubecon. This is where I get to really find out what their pain points are, what worked for them, what their recommendations are for MY problems. Project Pavillion I love hitting the project pavilion to talk to the newer projects in the sandbox and incubation tiers. KubeCon is the one place I can talk directly to maintainers about where their project is headed, what adoption looks like in the wild, and where the technical gaps are. Ricardo Rocha Why We Bet the Data Platform on Kubernetes – And How AI Is Changing How We Operate It A talk for end users… by end users. Day 2 operations is one area where automation and AI start having a very significant impact. Whether you already integrated agents in your ops stack, have them reporting and recommending actions, or are thinking about it, come and listen how others are doing it Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler An advanced topic but if you’re runnin...

blogs.title: The boundary problem in agentic AI is a platform problem
blogs.content: Posted on October 29, 2026 by William Rizzo (Field CTO, Kairos Maintainer, CNCF Ambassador) and Francesco Beltramini (Field CTO) An autonomous agent will do exactly what its tools let it do, and no more. This sounds like a constraint. In practice it is the whole risk, because the set of things an agent’s tools let it do is almost never the set anyone deliberately chose. It is the set that accumulated. A tool added for one workflow stays available for every workflow. A credential scoped for a demo survives into production. A delegation added to unblock a Friday deploy becomes a permanent edge in the graph. Nobody decides to give the agent that reach. There was never a moment where reach was decided at all. This is the pattern worth naming. It is not a bug in any particular agent framework and it will not be fixed by a better prompt. Across enough deployments the same shape recurs: authority is granted incrementally, locally, and invisibly, and the system’s actual power drifts steadily away from anyone’s model of what it should be able to do. The agents behave. The boundaries erode anyway. By the time someone asks “wait, can it do that?”, the honest answer is usually “it could for weeks, and we only noticed now.” The instinct is to treat this as a governance failure and answer with process and review boards. That instinct aims at the wrong layer. Process governs the decisions humans make. This problem is largely about the decisions nobody makes, the capabilities that arrive without a decision, and you cannot review a class of change that never surfaces as a change. What is needed is not more vigilance over the agent. It is a substrate that holds the line whether or not anyone is watching. Why the agent cannot hold its own boundary The tempting shortcut is to make the agent responsible for its own limits: tell it in its instructions what it may and may not do, and give it a sense of its own scope. This fails structurally, and the failure looks like success right up until it doesn’t. An agent’s output is a probability distribution over next actions, conditioned on context. It is not a guarantee. Most of the time the most probable action is the appropriate one, which is exactly what makes agents useful and exactly what makes them dangerous to trust. A boundary that holds ninety-nine times and yields on the hundredth is not a boundary; it is a strong suggestion with a failure rate. And the conditions that push an agent toward the edge of its instructions, novel inputs, adversarial phrasing, unusual state, are precisely the conditions where the boundary matters most and where probabilistic adherence is weakest. You rely on the mechanism least when you need it most. Underneath the reliability problem sits a harder one. Even a perfectly compliant agent, one that always did exactly what its instructions said, would still have whatever authority its tools and credentials actually grant. The instruction is a statement of intent. The tool binding is a statement of capability. When those two disagree, capability wins, because capability is what executes. An agent instructed not to move money, but holding a tool that moves money, is one clever prompt or one confused reasoning step away from moving money. The gap between intended scope and granted capability is the entire attack surface, and no amount of instruction closes it, because instruction and capability live in different layers and only one of them runs. So the boundary has to live where capability lives. Not in the agent’s reasoning, but in the infrastructure that decides what the agent’s reasoning is able to reach. Bounded autonomy is not a property of the agent. It is a property of the platform the agent runs on. The safe operating model Once the boundary belongs to the platform, the problem stops being novel. The industry has spent fifteen years learning to bound what a workload can do, because a microservice is also software that will do whatever its identity, network access, and permissions allow. We built a discipline around not trusting a workload to police itself. An agent is a workload. It is an unusually capable workload with a non-deterministic control loop, but the machinery that bounds workloads applies to it directly. The Safe Operating Model organizes that machinery as concentric rings of least privilege. Each ring binds one question about the agent, and each outer ring depends on the one inside it. The order is not decorative. Reach cannot be enforced without knowing what is connecting; capability cannot be enforced without knowing what is acting. Identity is the center because every other control resolves against it. The core: Identity Identity comes first because every other control depends on knowing what is acting. A workload identity standard issues each agent and each tool server a short-lived, attested credential. The platform no longer takes an agent’s word for what it is; it verifies. Every downstream decision, every reach check, every capability check, keys off this verified identity rather than a bearer token that can leak or be replayed. Get this wrong and the rest is built on sand. Get it right and the boundary has something real to attach to. Everything outward from here is an elaboration of a single question the core has already answered: what, exactly, is this. Ring 1: Reach With identity established, the first thing to bound is reach, meaning what the agent is permitted to connect to. A service mesh enforces this on the verified identity, per connection, independent of network topology. The agent may talk to the specific peers its work requires and to nothing else, and nothing else is the default rather than an afterthought. When an agent tries to reach a service it has no declared relationship with, the connection is refused before it opens. This is where the drift problem first meets a wall. A new edge in the agent’s reach cannot appear quietly at runtime, because reach is declared, and a change to a declaration is visible, reviewable, and attributable. The graph cannot grow in the dark. The accumulation that defined the original problem, one more connection, one more integration, no single one of them a decision, becomes a series of changes that each have to be made on purpose. Ring 2: Capability Reach controls who the agent can talk to. Capability controls what it can actually do, and this is where an agent’s autonomy cashes out: which tools it may invoke, and what it may do to the system. Two enforcement points matter, and they answer two different questions. The first is admission, which governs what capabilities the agent is allowed to hold. When the object that defines an agent’s permitted tools is a declarative resource in the cluster, policy can reject any attempt to bind a tool that was never approved, at the moment of the attempt, before the binding exists. An agent cannot acquire a capability that policy has not sanctioned, because the acquisition itself is what gets denied. A tool nobody reviewed cannot enter the system through the back door of an agent quietly adding it. The second is the call path, which governs what the agent may do with the capabilities it holds. Even among sanctioned tools, a gateway can authorize each individual invocation against the agent’s identity, so that a tool being present and reachable is not the same as a tool being callable. Ask for a tool outside the permitted set and the answer is a refusal, and the tool does not even appear in what the agent can see. Capability becomes something granted per action rather than something latent and waiting to be misused. Holding a tool and being allowed to use it, in a given moment, for a given task, are separated on purpose. The keystone One control sits above the rings and makes them coherent, and it is the one most easily forgotten. Every boundary described so far is expressed as configuration....
